text.p: The following are the main stories from Thursday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG
- Opposition Social Democrats (SPD) file complaint to Constitutional Court on government's 1996 budget.
- Ruling coalition wants to change law on atomic energy without help from SPD.
- Chambers of Industry and Commerce (DIHT) warn Germany will lose competitiveness if tax and economic policy are not reformed by this autumn.
- May industrial production declines 0.2 percent compared to April.
- German Farmers' Association says Finance Minister Theo Waigel plans to cut 1998 agricultural budget by 1.2 billion marks.
HANDELSBLATT
- Waigel plans to make savings by delaying repayment of some East German and state railway debts.
- German Institute for Economic Research (DIW) speak out against delay in European economic and monetary union.
- Eurocheque cards should be able to be used worldwide from next year, German banks say.
- Deutsche Telekom joins forces with Bertelsmann and Kirch in digital television.
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG
- Ministers block Waigel's plans for budget savings. Talks between Waigel and key spending ministries cannot end in consensus this week.
- Around 320,000 young people are without an apprenticeship, Federal Labour Office says.
- Cable television charges to rise, Deutsche Telekom says.
- DIW institute calls for higher deficit to fight unemployment.
DIE WELT
- Coalition plans 1997 budget with borrowing higher than investment.
- DIW predicts further rise in unemployment.
- Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt expects 20 million people to visit the Expo in Hanover in the year 2000.
